extracted.intended_audience: aspiring comedy writers who want to write for SNL / apply to NBC late-night writing programs
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, step-by-step guidance for producing an SNL application package and developing the skills, portfolio, and network required to be hired as a writer for Saturday Night Live (including applying to NBC's Late Night Writer’s Workshop).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application package requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To become a writer for SNL you need to complete and submit an application package on the SNL application website. The application to be an SNL writer includes a portfolio of original sketches, a bio, references, and demonstrated comedy writing experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the online submission form exactly when open; include bio, essay question responses, resume, and any required release forms. Submit the entire packet as a single PDF when requested. Include references and evidence of comedy writing experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binge watch (study) SNL
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch as much of the show as you can to notice patterns that you can use in your application and portfolio for becoming an SNL writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make notes of macro and micro patterns: themes of the sketches; character types or archetypes (e.g., morally gray characters); word choice; type of humor; plot of the sketches; conflict; what types of sketches seem to work best (past and current season); setting; number of characters; and the big idea (the compelling idea behind the sketch). Use historical knowledge of the show to inform your writing and submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study (a.k.a. stalk) SNL writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Research other SNL writers' public work and presence — websites, social media, blogs, podcasts, interviews and videos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow them, read their articles, listen to podcasts, watch interviews and their videos. Engage with positive social etiquette (follow, share, be polite—'network, but don’t be creepy'). You may pick up tidbits that give you an edge in your application or interview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the funny / continuous learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Bone up on comedy by reading humor writing books, blogs, watching videos, and taking comedy courses (online or in-person).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended resources include: The Serious Guide To Joke Writing; Poking a Dead Frog; Comedy Writing for Late-Night TV; Truth In Comedy; The Comedy Bible; And Here’s The Kicker; Step by Step to Stand-Up Comedy; How To Write Funny; The Complete Idiot's Guide to Writing Comedy; The Comic Toolbox; The Hidden Tools Of Comedy. Consider free online comedy classes and paid offerings like Steve Martin’s MasterClass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write funny stuff (produce a variety of comedic work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write jokes, sketches, stand-up material, dialogue, parodies, remotes, articles, blog posts, YouTube scripts, social media posts — anything that exercises your comedic muscles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a running collection of funny words, sayings, situations, character traits and jokes. Publish material to get real-world feedback and engagement analytics (e.g., on Twitter, YouTube, Medium) to beef up your resume and portfolio. Use notetaking/voice apps to capture ideas. Scale up strengths and work on weaknesses based on audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write standup material (SNL writer style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many SNL writers write and perform stand-up; develop a 5-minute set, perform at open-mics and refine the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record performances, analyze which jokes hit or bomb, observe laughter spikes, hone delivery, and collect video of successful performances as 'portfolio gold' to show ability to own a crowd. Standup also teaches confessional honesty and human truth that informs sketch characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop funny characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Create and refine comedic characters that make other people laugh and often don’t see how funny they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test characters in stand-up routines or sketches, keep detailed notes on character traits and appearance, and remember characters don’t have to be human. Use performances to fine-tune character details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare 3–5 original SNL sketches
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a submission packet with roughly 3–5 original sketches demonstrating range and fit for SNL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shoot for variety (commercial parody, topical/pop-culture or political, and other sketches showing range). Include different themes, characters, and types of humor. Insider tip: include names of active SNL cast members and potential hosts as characters in your sketches. Aim to show what 'sticks' with reviewers and recruiters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get an agent
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain a talent agent to help connect you to opportunities and people in the industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a professional portfolio first. Seek an agent with New York connections or an agent who specializes in TV writers; agents can share insider tips and open doors to NBC or SNL contacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tap into your inner pain (use authenticity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use personal pain and honest human experience as material — pain is an essential element in humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage universal experiences and vulnerability to connect with audiences; many comedy teachers emphasize that comedy and tragedy are linked (quotes from Charlie Chaplin and Gilbert Gottfried illustrate this point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply for the NBC Late Night Writer’s Workshop
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply to the annual NBCUniversal Late Night & Alternative Writer’s Workshop (a multi-day NYC program that exposes sketch and comedy writers to late-night shows and readies them for staff writer positions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The workshop can lead to meeting executives, experiencing a writers' room, and making connections. Study the workshop's specific application rules closely (submit as a single PDF, complete bio, essay, resume, sign release forms, include letters of recommendation). Follow the workshop's social media for open submission periods and details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double check everything (proofread & get feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoroughly proofread your application materials and have others review them before submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check names, spellings, punctuation, times and dates. Use editing tools (e.g., Grammarly) and run the application by experienced writers, mentors, or your talent agent to avoid simple errors that could disqualify you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit the application and wait actively
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit your completed application when the submission window opens, then engage in 'active waiting' rather than passive waiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the SNL Writer Application website and workshop social accounts for open submission announcements. After submitting, continue writing, studying, performing, publishing, and improving your skills while you wait (responses may take up to four weeks or more).

rubrics_metrics.name: Network respectfully and gain inside perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend live show tapings, meet people in the industry when possible, and build professional relationships respectfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing the show live gives an insider’s perspective and motivation. Network but maintain polite, positive etiquette and social distancing (‘don’t be creepy’). Follow industry social media accounts (Late Night Writer’s Workshop, NBCunitips) to stay in the loop.
